what: The frame the open list called an outlier, measured against its neighbours instead of against a median
the_claim_being_checked: one frame at 34,6 dB where its clip sits at 44,4 -- the last thing in the sparse work that had not been explained, and the only remaining open item about the decoder itself rather than about coverage or a vendor tool
where_it_is: Extraction (2020), frame 63325. It was described alongside Glass Onion, whose sparse frames carry no steep object at all and measure 50 to 68 dB from four different clip windows; the frame in question is in another title
what_the_frame_is: sparse, steep and coarse at once: fifteen objects all three, in a clip that carries 15 sparse, 240 steep and 45 coarse objects

the_two_readings_it_could_have_been.reading: both corrections are doing work on this frame and neither alternative is better: as decoded 34,55 dB, with the printed steep reading 18,43, with the printed sparse reading 7,54, with both 1,05 -- which is the figure the first round recorded before any of them. Dither is not it either: 34,90 with dither off

and_then_the_question_that_settles_it.method: rank every frame of the window by the same measure, instead of comparing one frame with a median

conclusion: there is no outlier. Frame 63325 is the tenth worst of 99 frames in the window it was measured in and the forty-eighth of 299 in a wider one, in a passage where this decoder and Dolby's agree less well throughout -- the window sits at 40 to 42 dB where Extraction 2's sparse clip sits at 46,78 and Glass Onion's at 58. A frame six decibels under its window's median, with forty-seven frames beneath it, is not something left to explain
the_mistake: comparing one frame with a clip median and never asking where it ranked among its neighbours. A median says what a typical frame does; it says nothing about the spread, and this passage's spread runs from 21 to 60 dB
